opus_only: Because the premia and their correlations appear in non-equity asset classes, theories built for U.S. stocks alone cannot fully explain them.
Authors disclose a commercial interest: their employer/consultancy invests in value and momentum strategies.
The global three-factor model prices the Fama-French U.S. stock portfolios and hedge fund indices well.
Value positions are contrarian, hence less crowded.
Whether these flow/delegation models can match the empirical magnitudes is unresolved.
The 90%-of-cap U.S. universe averages the largest 17% of firms, an extremely liquid, tradeable set.
Country index returns, prices and book values come from MSCI and Bloomberg.
Value and momentum are stronger in small stocks in this period (Hong-Lim-Stein, Grinblatt-Moskowitz, Fama-French 2012) but the size relation is not robust for momentum in other periods.
Prior work shows stronger value and momentum in less liquid emerging markets (Rouwenhorst 1998, Erb-Harvey 2006, Griffin-Ji-Martin 2003).
Currency universe: 10 currencies (AUD, CAD, DEM/EUR, JPY, NZD, NOK, SEK, CHF, GBP, USD) from Datastream spot rates, Jan 1979-Jul 2011, min 7.
Currency returns are USD-denominated from forwards (or spot plus Libor differential), so they include carry.
Bond returns from Bloomberg and Morgan Markets; short rates and 10-year yields from Bloomberg.
Inflation forecasts come from Consensus Economics analyst surveys (used in the alternative real-yield bond value measure).
Simple measures likely understate the returns available from better-designed value and momentum signals.
The value+momentum combination's pricing results are insensitive to whether price is lagged in the value measure.
Better stock value measures exist (Lakonishok-Shleifer-Vishny, Asness-Porter-Stevens, Piotroski) but BE/ME is kept for simplicity and consistency.
The same MOM2-12 signal is used in every asset class.
Behavioral and flow theories (DHS, BSV, Hong-Stein, Vayanos-Woolley) predict a link between long-term returns and book-to-market.
Goyal-Wahal: across 36 countries, 7-12 vs 2-6 month returns differ significantly only in the U.S.
MOM2-12 is kept because it is the established signal with out-of-sample success; MOM7-12 should not change conclusions.
Authors assert alternative momentum windows (MOM7-12) would not change conclusions, without showing results.
Stock tercile portfolios are value-weighted by beginning-of-month cap; non-stock portfolios are equal-weighted.
3 terciles x 2 signals x 8 asset classes = 48 new test portfolios.
Table I returns are excess of the 1-month U.S. T-bill rate, with t-stats, stdev and Sharpe ratios, annualized from monthly series.
Value-momentum correlations in Table I are computed on returns after removing the asset-class market (residuals).
All statistics are annualized from monthly returns.
In non-stock asset classes portfolios are equal-weighted and the same tercile/rank-factor/combo construction is applied.
Panel C tests alternative bond value measures over Jan 1983-Jul 2011 (vs. Jan 1982 start given for the bond data).

Bond value as the real yield (10-year yield minus 5-year inflation forecast) works much better: P3-P1 2.0% (t=3.78, SR 0.73), factor 1.9% (t=3.58, SR 0.70); correlation with momentum near zero (-0.09/-0.03).

A composite of the three bond value measures is strongest: P3-P1 2.6% (t=4.88, SR 0.91), factor 2.9% (t=5.89, SR 1.10, alpha 2.6% t=5.48); correlation with momentum ~0 (0.03/0.04); combo factor SR 0.81.
The combination's higher Sharpe ratio raises the bar for theories explaining value or momentum alone.
Even in Japan a positive momentum weight improves the efficient frontier (confirmed by static portfolio optimization).
Cap-weighting or equal-weighting markets gives nearly identical results; equal-vol is used for consistency with non-equity classes where market cap has no meaning.
Applying value and momentum jointly across asset classes sets an asset-pricing hurdle several times larger than U.S. equity data.
Bonds are the weakest asset class: baseline value and momentum premia are not statistically reliable.
Averaging several value measures diversifies measurement error and gives more reliable premia (Israel-Moskowitz 2012 for stocks).
Table II diagonals are the average correlation of each market's strategy with the average of the same strategy in all other markets (leave-one-out).
An F-test checks joint significance; * marks 5% significance.
Average stock value strategy correlates 0.68 with value in other stock markets and 0.15 with non-stock value.
Average stock momentum correlates 0.65 with momentum in other stock markets and 0.37 with non-stock momentum.

Value in one stock market correlates -0.53 with momentum in other stock markets; stock value vs non-stock momentum -0.26; non-stock value vs stock momentum -0.16; non-stock value vs non-stock momentum -0.13.
The first principal component loads with one sign on every value strategy and the opposite sign on every momentum strategy.
U.K. stocks: Sharpe 0.38/0.48/1.07, corr -0.62; Europe stocks: 0.54/0.75/1.20, corr -0.55; both show the 1999-2000 value drawdown offset by momentum, and a momentum fall around 2009.

Japan stocks: Sharpe value 0.77, momentum 0.13, combo 0.88, corr -0.64; momentum is roughly flat over 1972-2011 while value rises strongly, with a value drawdown around 1999-2000 coinciding with a momentum spike.

Fixed income (Figure 2): Sharpe value 0.07, momentum 0.17, combo 0.20, corr -0.35; bond value has a deep cumulative loss from the mid-1980s to the early-mid 1990s and ends near zero, so bond results are fragile and period-dependent.
Global stocks (Figure 2): Sharpe value 0.51, momentum 0.59, combo 1.28, corr -0.60; value's 1999-2000 drawdown is visible even in the global aggregate.
Global macro regressors are GDP-weighted averages across US, UK, Europe, Japan using ECRI data and recession dates; market is MSCI World excess return; TERM and DEF are U.S. versions only.
Momentum does worse in recessions, especially outside stocks (nonstock momentum recession coef -0.0081, t=-2.44; all-asset -0.0072, t=-2.26).
DEF loads positively on global stock value (0.265, t=2.86) but insignificantly negatively on non-stock value.
Griffin-Ji-Martin (2003) show macro risk models cannot explain momentum across 40 countries.
Table III does not report intercepts, so how much of the premia macro variables absorb is not shown.
Recession dummy is defined from NBER (U.S.) or ECRI (other countries) peak/trough dates, coded 0 = peak and 1 = trough.

Table III global columns: global stock momentum DEF -0.375 (t=-3.87); nonstock value TERM -0.0885 (t=-3.30); all-asset value TERM -0.0551 (t=-2.23), all-asset momentum DEF -0.149 (t=-2.84); market betas small and insignificant; R2 2.3-6.4%.
The Fama-French DEF factor return loads negatively on momentum in every asset group.
All spreads are sign-flipped so that higher values mean more liquidity.
Liquidity regressions cover Jan 1987-Jul 2011 only (shorter than the 1972 return sample).
Global liquidity measures average the four countries' measures with weights from each country's first-principal-component contribution; all regressions control for Table III macro variables.

U.S. funding liquidity PC: value -0.0111 (t=-2.89), momentum +0.0153 (t=3.31), Val-Mom -0.0264 (t=-3.41); TED: value -0.0052 (-1.44), momentum 0.0129 (3.07); all-liquidity PC: value -0.0154 (-2.84), momentum 0.0195 (2.96).
U.S. market liquidity shocks (on/off-the-run, Pastor-Stambaugh, market PC) are insignificant for value and momentum; only Acharya-Pedersen is marginal (value 0.0010, t=2.02).

With U.S. measures the 50/50 combo is not fully liquidity-neutral: it loads positively on TED (0.0061, t=2.13), swap-T-bill (0.0104, t=3.67) and Acharya-Pedersen (0.0013, t=3.05), though not on the funding PC (t=1.49) or all PC (t=1.09).
Global LIBOR-term repo: value -0.0177 (t=-2.87), momentum 0.0139 (t=1.66); global swap-T-bill value -0.0076 (t=-2.15); global TED value -0.0067 (-1.69), momentum 0.0094 (2.00).
Each liquidity shock enters a separate regression (with macro controls); dependent variables are global value and momentum everywhere factors, the 50/50 combo and value minus momentum.
Adding liquidity shocks barely changes macro coefficients.
Some liquidity measures need tick data or prime-broker balance sheets unavailable outside the U.S., limiting the global liquidity proxies.
Figure 3 caption gives Jan 1987-Jun 2010, while the text says the index is plotted Jan 1987-Jul 2011 (internal inconsistency).
Market liquidity shocks show little relation to value and momentum returns.
Forced liquidations from cash needs, redemptions and risk management hit crowded momentum trades harder than value trades; further investigation is left for future work.
Liquidity risk can only partially explain the cross-section of returns because it cannot explain the combo's profitability.
Equation (4) is estimated separately for each of the 8 markets on its 6 tercile portfolios (48 test assets).
No joint test of pricing errors is possible for equation (4) because regressors differ by market.
Because test assets and factors share no securities, the fit evidences genuine common global factor structure.
Figure 5 scatter: most test assets lie near the 45-degree line; the largest misses include low-return commodity value and bond momentum portfolios below the line.
Cross-market explanatory power shows the common variation is economically meaningful, capturing much of the cross-section of average returns.
The three-factor fit is mechanically helped by overlap between test assets and factors, unlike equation (4).

Even the best (AMP) model is rejected by the GRS test (p = 0) on the 48 portfolios; remaining misfits include low-return momentum and value portfolios in bonds, currencies and commodities (read from chart).
In Figure 6 each model must also price the equity premium; the AMP model's value/momentum factors are inverse in-sample-volatility weighted across the eight asset classes.
Global factors built mostly from other markets explain the 50 Fama-French U.S. size-value and size-momentum portfolios with R2 0.64 and 18 bp mean absolute alpha.
Market beta uses the Dimson correction (contemporaneous plus 1- and 2-month lagged market) to handle nonsynchronous trading.
TERM and DEF betas carry 21 and 23 bp/month premia, but are subsumed when liquidity betas are added; GDP and LRCG betas are not priced.
VAL and MOM everywhere betas capture average returns and subsume much of liquidity risk's explanatory power.
Using factor-mimicking portfolios makes the macro/liquidity factors traded returns so GRS time-series tests are valid.

Table VI caption says factor-mimicking portfolios come from cross-sectional coefficients in Table IV, but the text and Table V show they come from the Fama-MacBeth regressions in Table V (labelling inconsistency).
Eig% = sum of eigenvalues of model-implied covariance / sum of eigenvalues of sample covariance (share of covariance captured).
Adding the liquidity factor-mimicking portfolio cuts mean absolute alpha to 31 bp and raises fit, but GRS still rejects.
Measurement error in liquidity proxies may understate liquidity's explanatory power.
One liquidity factor cannot price both negatively correlated positive-premium strategies unless betas/premia vary strongly over time.
Dropping either VAL or MOM from the model worsens fit considerably, showing both factors are needed.
Hedge fund returns load on global value and momentum, implying these factors are a natural benchmark for hedge fund performance.
Some studies find equity momentum's net returns and capacity much lower than paper returns.
Shorting is costless-symmetric in futures but costly in stocks, a potential implementation concern.
Frazzini-Israel-Moskowitz find institutional shorting costs similar to buying/selling and not prohibitive.
The paper is framed as an out-of-sample test of U.S. stock anomalies in other asset classes, hence deliberately simple choices.
Alternative weighting schemes give similar results; trading costs unlikely to change much given the liquid universe.
Bonds remain the weakest asset class with the uniform measures; composite measures (Table I Panel C) improve them markedly.
Authors judge the effects applicable to real portfolios, citing the hedge-fund pricing evidence.
Value-momentum correlation became more negative (-0.44 to -0.63), offsetting higher within-style correlations so the combo Sharpe was stable.
Rising correlations may reflect growing arbitrageur participation in global value/momentum.

Table VII labels the second half 1992-2010 while the text says 1992-2011; Sharpe levels (combo 1.40/1.43) match Table I P3-P1 (1.42) rather than the rank factors (1.59), so the portfolio type is unstated.
Improving/worsening liquidity regimes are the top/bottom half of global liquidity shock observations (caption cites Table III though shocks are defined with Table IV).
Correlations within value and within momentum rose significantly over time, and value-momentum correlation became more negative.
The correlation increase is a post-1998 regime shift rather than a gradual trend, and liquidity effects on correlations exist only after 1998.
Funding liquidity and limits to arbitrage may be increasingly important drivers of value/momentum after 1998, more than growing popularity per se.
sonnet_only: A three-factor model (global market, global value, global momentum) prices the 48 test assets, Fama-French US portfolios and hedge fund indices.
The simple three-factor model is motivated by increasingly global finance and a wish for one model for all asset classes rather than specialised models.
Table I frames the main claim: value and momentum, alone and combined, work in every market, including new evidence for bonds (value and momentum) and value in currencies and commodities.
Table I Panel C tests alternative bond value measures (real yield, term spread, composite).
Single uniform signal per style across eight markets minimises data mining; results are positive in every class but bonds are statistically insignificant.
Table II examines cross-asset-class correlation of value and momentum returns; the strength of comovement can support or challenge theoretical explanations.
Macro exposure test: regress value and momentum returns (US stocks, global stocks, nonstock, all assets) on macro variables (Table III).

Table IV Panel A (US liquidity measures, with Table III macro controls): funding liquidity shocks load negatively on value and positively on momentum. TED spread: value -0.0052 (t -1.44), momentum 0.0129 (3.07), combo 0.0061 (2.13), value-minus-momentum -0.0180 (-2.62); funding PC: value -0.0111 (-2.89), momentum 0.0153 (3.31), combo 0.0042 (1.49), Val-Mom -0.0264 (-3.41); All PC: value -0.0154 (-2.84), momentum 0.0195 (2.96), combo 0.0043 (1.09), Val-Mom -0.0349 (-3.17). Market liquidity measures are weak.
This 'other markets' test has no security overlap between test assets and factors, avoiding the usual mechanical link in single-market asset pricing tests.

Table VI time-series pricing tests regress the 48 portfolios (plus 25+25 US portfolios and 13 hedge fund indices) on factor-mimicking portfolios from Table V and on global/US factor sets, reporting GRS, average |alpha|, cross-sectional R2, average time-series R2 and Eig% (Moskowitz 2003).
Models with only value or only momentum increase pricing errors and reduce fit, underscoring that one factor cannot explain both.
